title: Acts of Possession on the Pacific Coast
subtitle: Claiming ceremonies on the Pacific coast from Balboa to Sloat, 1513 to 1846, with the manuscript record for every act
abstract: Every documented claiming ceremony on the Pacific coast of the Americas, from Balboa wading into the Gulf of San Miguel in 1513 to Sloat's flag at Monterey in 1846. Spanish acts followed a prescribed legal script. By 1773 it was literally a fill-in-the-blanks form, the viceregal formulario (AGN, Historia 68; trans. Servín, CHSQ 40:3): the Te Deum on the beach, a proclamation 'in a loud voice' in the king's name under the bull of 1493, branches cut and stones moved 'without encountering opposition,' a cross planted on a cairn with a duplicate of the notarized act sealed in a bottle beneath it. Rival empires answered with their own legal theaters: England with consent ceremonies and an engraved plate, Russia with buried plates, a double-headed eagle, and a signed record of Kashaya consent, the United States with proclamation by conquest. Every pinned act is documented in its manuscripts or scholarly editions; candidates whose attestation remains secondhand or contested are held back in the research files rather than mapped. Census compiled from Servín (1961, 1963), Wagner (PHR 1938; CHSQ 1924-1930), Bolton, Engelhardt, Beals, Howay, Orth, and the AGI, AGN, AHN and Library of Congress records; each entry carries its archival signature and published text.
legend_note: Ceremonies sharing one shore carry small display offsets, noted per entry with the documented coordinates. Documented but unlocatable, so not pinned: Iturbi (Cardona pearl expedition), gulf coast of Baja California, c. 1615 (Servín n.30; AGI Guadalajara 133; Patronato 20, N.5, R.18); Porter y Casanate, 'various unknown ports' of the Gulf, 1648-49 (AGI Guadalajara 134); two further 1788 Martínez-Haro anchorages (AHN Estado 4289). Entries whose attestation remains secondhand or contested are held in the research files pending verification rather than mapped.

features.name: Toma de posesión of the Mar del Sur (and Golfo de San Miguel, named 25 Sept)

date.display: 1513-09-29 (St Michael's day; first sight and naming of the gulf 1513-09-25; further autos de posesión around the gulf in October 1513)

features.summary: Per Oviedo (who read and later held Valderrábano's original testimonio): at vespers, as the tide rose, Balboa took in hand a banner/pendón real painted with the Virgin and Child above the royal arms of Castile and León, and with naked sword and shield waded knee-deep into the salt water, pacing about and proclaiming: «Vivan los muy altos é muy poderosos Reyes don Fernando é doña Johana...

quotes.text: Vivan los muy altos é muy poderosos Reyes don Fernando é doña Johana... en cuyo nombre é por la corona real de Castilla tomo é aprehendo la possesion real é corporal é actualmente destas mares é tierras é costas é puertos é islas australes...  [In whose name, and for the royal Crown of Castile, I take and seize real and corporeal and actual possession of these seas and lands and coasts and ports and southern islands.]
quotes.cite: Oviedo, Historia general y natural de las Indias, lib. XXIX, cap. III (ed. Amador de los Ríos, III, 13). Oviedo read and copied the lost notarial testimonio of Andrés de Valderrábano; translation A.C.

facts: Vasco Núñez de Balboa with 26 picked men (among them Francisco Pizarro); escribano real Andrés de Valderrábano, who drew the testimonio; priest Andrés de Vera. The roll of the 67 'primeros chripstianos que vieron la mar del Sur' was recorded by Valderrábano on 25 Sept. Days earlier Alonso Martín de Don Benito had been the first to enter the sea in a canoe (his 1535 Lima probanza attests the possession).

features.name: Revillagigedo Islands (Isla Santo Tomás = Socorro), Pacific off Mexico; edge of the censu

date.display: 26 Dec 1533 (anchored Christmas Day; act the following afternoon)

features.summary: Grijalva's San Lázaro expedition anchored on Christmas Day 1533; the captain took possession in person the following afternoon on Isla Santo Tomás (Socorro); a cross planted with a parchment escrito recording the arrival. No notary is named: the record is the expedition derrotero, preserved in a Muñoz copy. The act covered Santo Tomás alone; the northern islets were merely named Los Inocentes.

features.summary: Per Unamuno's relación: on a hill near the shore strewn with pearl-oyster shells, 'as it seemed to be a suitable place to take possession in His Majesty's name of the port and the country, seeing that I and the rest of the party had landed and traversed the country round about... quietly and pacifically, as in territory belonging to his domain, I did so in the name of King Philip, our master, in due legal form, through Diego Vasquez Mexia...

features.name: Puerto de San Sebastián / Villa de San Felipe / Reino de Nueva Andalucía

date.display: 1596-09-04 (circa; ceremony 'otro día' after the 3 Sept landfall per Vizcaíno's relación; expedition stayed at the bay 3-10 Sept 1596)

features.summary: Per Vizcaíno's own relación (quoted verbatim in Mathes): a tent town with streets and plaza was laid out; the next day, before ~200 Indians, 'con la solemnidad que se requería hincado el estandarte Real en tierra tomé possessión de ella en el nombre de Su Magestad y púsele por nombre a la Villa San Phillipe, al Puerto San Sebastián y el Reyno Nueba Andaluzía.' At the possession the friars said mass at an altar ashore, carrying the image of Nuestra Señora in procession from the beach; an Indian principal with ~800 followers knelt before the image. Large crosses were left standing when the expedition departed.
facts: Sebastián Vizcaíno (general, performed the act personally); Fray Francisco de Balda (Franciscan commissary) and four other Franciscans (mass, procession of the image of Our Lady); Captain Rodrigo de Figueroa (lieutenant, left in command of the town); notary not named in the sources consulted.

date.display: 1598-04-30 (Feast of the Ascension)

features.summary: Solemn high mass, sermon, blessing of the royal standard, then Oñate read the long written act: 'En el nombre de la Santísima Trinidad...', taking 'la tenencia y posesión real y actual, civil y natural, una, dos y tres veces... en este dicho Río del Norte, sin exceptuar cosa alguna' of all the kingdoms and provinces of New Mexico for Philip II, with a cross raised and the requerimiento framework invoked; notarized by Pérez de Donís; feasting and a comedy followed ('the first Thanksgiving' tradition). A written, witnessed, notarized instrument survives.

features.name: Founding and formal possession of the site of the Real Presidio de Santa Bárbara
features.summary: Timber cut for a large cross, a hut-chapel and altar table; Serra blessed the ground and the Holy Cross, which was raised and venerated; first mass attended by governor, officers and troops; sermon; per Palóu the ceremony concluded 'by the formal act of taking possession of the site, without the slightest opposition on the part of the natives'; Bancroft (from Neve's and Serra's letters) records mass and a chanted alabado on 21 April. features.name: Vancouver at Possession Sound
features.summary: On 4 June 1792, George III's birthday, the crews were served a double allowance of grog to drink the king's health and Vancouver went ashore about one o'clock with Broughton and his officers, 'pursuing the usual formalities' and under a royal salute from the vessels. He took possession of the coast from New Albion in latitude 39 degrees 20 minutes north to the entrance of the supposed strait of Juan de Fuca, naming the interior sea the Gulf of Georgia and the continent binding it New Georgia. The branch of Admiralty Inlet where it was done he named Possession Sound. The ceremony came two years after the Nootka Convention was supposed to have closed the age of such acts.
facts: George Vancouver (England); with Lt. W. R. Broughton and officers ashore
royal salute from the vessels, the usual formalities performed ashore, the king’s health drunk, possession declared from 39°20′N to the Fuca entrance, New Georgia and Possession Sound named
